item.title: Elder Eraka: “O Eraka, painful are sensual pleasures! O Eraka, not happiness are sensual pleasures! One who desires sensual pleasures, desires suffering. One who does…
item.description:
Elder Eraka:
“O Eraka, painful are sensual pleasures!
O Eraka, not happiness are sensual pleasures!
One who desires sensual pleasures, desires suffering.
One who does not desire sensual pleasures, does not desire suffering.
O Eraka, know this as it is.”

From: Theragāthā 1.93

item.title: “Monks, the eye is burning. Forms are burning. Eye-consciousness is burning. Eye-contact is burning. Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact — whether pleasant, painful, or…
item.description:
“Monks, the eye is burning. Forms are burning. Eye-consciousness is burning. Eye-contact is burning. Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact — whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is burning. Burning with what? Burning with the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. I say it is burning with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. The ear … The nose … The tongue is burning. Tastes are burning. Tongue-consciousness is burning. Tongue-contact is burning … The body … The mind is burning. Phenomena are burning. Mind-consciousness is burning. Mind-contact is burning. Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact … that feeling is burning. Burning with the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. I say it is burning with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.28

item.title: “Venerable sir, what is the first jhāna?” “Here, venerable sir, a monk, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the…
item.description:
“Venerable sir, what is the first jhāna?” “Here, venerable sir, a monk, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, venerable sir, is called the first jhāna.” “Venerable sir, how many factors does the first jhāna have?” “Venerable sir, the first jhāna has five factors. Here, a monk in the first jhāna has initial thought, sustained thought, rapture, pleasure, and unification of mind. Thus, venerable sir, the first jhāna has five factors.” “Venerable sir, how many factors does the first jhāna abandon and how many does it possess?” “Venerable sir, the first jhāna abandons five factors and possesses five factors. Here, a monk in the first jhāna has abandoned sensual desire, abandoned ill-will, abandoned sloth and torpor, abandoned restlessness and remorse, abandoned doubt; he possesses initial thought, sustained thought, rapture, pleasure, and unification of mind. Thus, venerable sir, the first jhāna abandons five factors and possesses five factors.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 43 – Mahāvedallasutta

item.title: “Short is this life — Within a hundred years one dies, And even if one lives longer, One dies of old age. People grieve for…
item.description:
“Short is this life —
Within a hundred years one dies,
And even if one lives longer,
One dies of old age.

People grieve for what they hold as ‘mine’ —
All possessions are impermanent.
Seeing this, one should live homeless.

What people think of as ‘mine’
Is destroyed by death.
Knowing this, the wise one
Would not incline toward ‘mine.’

As when a person wakes up,
He no longer sees what appeared in a dream,
So too, a beloved person who dies
Is no longer seen.

Those who are seen and heard
Are called by such and such a name —
Only the name remains
For one who has passed away.

People who are greedy for ‘mine’
Do not abandon sorrow, lamentation,
And stinginess.
Therefore, sages, leaving behind attachments,
Live seeing safety.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 4.6

item.title: “Monks, I will teach you about suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Listen.…
item.description:
“Monks, I will teach you about suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Listen. And what, monks, is suffering? It should be said: the five aggregates of clinging. What five? The form aggregate of clinging … the consciousness aggregate of clinging. This, monks, is called suffering. And what, monks, is the origin of suffering? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence … craving for non-existence. This, monks, is called the origin of suffering. And what, monks, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the abandoning and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance. This, monks, is called the cessation of suffering. And what, monks, is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view … right concentration. This, monks, is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.104
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, these five things, when developed and cultivated, lead to the destruction of the defilements. What five? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating foulness in…
item.description:
“Monks, these five things, when developed and cultivated, lead to the destruction of the defilements. What five? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating foulness in the body, with the perception of disgust for food, with the perception of non-delight in the entire world, contemplating impermanence in all formations, and the perception of death is well established within him. These five things, monks, when developed and cultivated, lead to the destruction of the defilements.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.70

item.title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline, as heedlessness. For one who is…
item.description:
“I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline, as heedlessness. For one who is heedless, monks, unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.58

item.title: “Here, monks, the third kind of ascetics and brahmins think: ‘Those first ascetics and brahmins … have not escaped Māra’s power. Suppose we make a…
item.description:
“Here, monks, the third kind of ascetics and brahmins think: ‘Those first ascetics and brahmins … have not escaped Māra’s power. Suppose we make a hiding place near the bait cast by Māra and the world’s offerings. Having made a hiding place, without entering, without indulging, we will eat the bait and the world’s offerings. By not entering, not indulging, we will not become infatuated; not infatuated, we will not become heedless; not heedless, we will not become subject to Māra’s will among that bait and offerings.’ These ascetics and brahmins make a hiding place near the bait and offerings. Having done so, without entering, without indulging, they eat the bait and offerings. Not entering, not indulging, they do not become infatuated; not infatuated, they do not become heedless; not heedless, they do not become subject to Māra’s will. But then they have such wrong views as: ‘The world is eternal; the world is not eternal; the world is finite; the world is infinite …’ Thus, monks, these third ascetics and brahmins have not escaped Māra’s power.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 25 – Nivāpasutta

item.title: “Ānanda, those noble thoughts that are conducive to progress and lead to the complete destruction of suffering — such as renunciation thoughts, non-ill-will thoughts, harmlessness…
item.description:
“Ānanda, those noble thoughts that are conducive to progress and lead to the complete destruction of suffering — such as renunciation thoughts, non-ill-will thoughts, harmlessness thoughts — he reflects: ‘I will think these thoughts.’ In this way, he is clearly aware of that.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 122 – Mahāsuññatasutta

item.title: “Sensual desire, monks, is an obscuration, a hindrance, a covering of the mind, debilitating to wisdom. Ill-will, monks … sloth and torpor … restlessness and…
item.description:
“Sensual desire, monks, is an obscuration, a hindrance, a covering of the mind, debilitating to wisdom. Ill-will, monks … sloth and torpor … restlessness and remorse … doubt is an obscuration, a hindrance, a covering of the mind, debilitating to wisdom. These, monks, are the five obscurations, hindrances, coverings of the mind, debilitating to wisdom.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.51
